business_question: You are supporting a New York Times editor who is fact-checking a reporter's proposed statement that the Titanic evacuation followed a 'women and children first' practice. Using the supplied Titanic passenger dataset, determine what the data show about the relationship between sex and survival. Give a numerical answer using survivor counts, survival rates, the percentage-point difference, and the relative survival rate. Create one chart illustrating the result for the editor. Distinguish an observed association from proof that a particular evacuation policy or order caused the result, and identify briefly what this dataset alone cannot establish.
business_answer_shown: In the supplied 1,309 passenger records, 339 of 466 female passengers survived (72.7%), compared with 161 of 843 male passengers (19.1%). Female survival was 53.6 percentage points higher; the female-to-male survival-rate ratio was 3.81. This verifies the sex-survival association only. Child prioritization was not tested, and these data alone cannot establish evacuation decisions, intentions, causes, or whether a policy was followed. The chart preserves the editor's question and provides the same bounded evidence for the case's maritime safety review board.

data_fidelity_checks.check: Passenger records, fields, encodings, and inclusion
data_fidelity_checks.notes: Inspected every record in Titanic.xlsx, Sheet1, rows 2-1310. Fields are pclass, survived, name, sex, age, embarked, and home.dest. Sex contains female (466) and male (843); survived is a binary integer indicator, interpreted as 1=survived and 0=did not survive, consistent with the baseline. Neither field contains missing or ambiguous values. No blank or identical duplicate records were found. All 1,309 records were included without recoding or exclusion; missing values in unrelated fields did not affect eligibility.
Female: 339 survived and 127 did not, total 466. Male: 161 survived and 682 did not, total 843. Denominators sum to 1,309; survivors sum to 500; nonsurvivors sum to 809.

339/466 x 100 = 72.7467811159%; 161/843 x 100 = 19.0984578885%. Subtraction of unrounded percentage rates gives 53.6483232274 percentage points. (339/466)/(161/843) = 3.8090395330, female divided by male. Displayed rates and difference round to one decimal place; the ratio rounds to two. Percentage points and multiplicative rate ratio are kept distinct.

data_fidelity_checks.notes: Female precedes male, with a common zero baseline and a 0%-100% scale. Visible bar heights agree approximately with the verified 72.7% and 19.1%; no consequential value error was detected. Exact baseline values cannot be read because numeric bar labels are absent.

Recomputed the same records for the rerun. Both bar heights use unrounded rates on a shared 0%-100% scale. Verified category-to-value pairing, 339/466 and 161/843 labels, 72.7% and 19.1% rate labels, the 53.6-percentage-point title, directed 3.81-times ratio, population label, source, and rounding note.

Separated the sex-survival association, child prioritization, and existence or causal effect of an evacuation practice or order. Only the first component is tested. First-run weakness: a generic causal limitation omitted explicit disclosure that child prioritization was untested. Revised a local working copy of the specialist instruction to require component-by-component on-chart disclosure, then reran the same case. The final chart names the untested child component and states that decisions, intentions, causes, and whether a policy was followed cannot be established. The supplied packet remains unchanged; no age analysis was added.

Inspected all eighteen elements using qualitative YES/NO judgments, with Tables not applicable. Each of the five NO findings has a separate assessment entry; all eighteen judgments appear across the six comparison entries. Compared baseline and improved charts side by side and inspected the final chart at 1,522 x 892 and 761 x 446 pixels and in grayscale. Labels and notes remain readable with no clipping or overlap. These are inspection judgments, not measured usability scores.

remaining_limitations: The association alone cannot establish an evacuation policy or order, the decision process, intentions, or causes of the survival difference. Independent historical evidence would be needed for those claims.
Child prioritization was not tested; an age-based analysis is outside this existing sex-survival chart improvement task.

The supplied workbook does not document provenance or coverage sufficiently to establish representativeness or justify generalization beyond its 1,309 records, including application to modern evacuation training.
Rates and the difference are rounded to one decimal place and the relative rate to two; bars use unrounded values.
The rerun fixes the first draft's missing child-scope disclosure, but inspection does not replace an editor's or domain expert's review or a measured reader-comprehension study.
abstention_or_more_information_needed: No additional information is needed to verify and improve the supplied sex-survival comparison. Abstain from concluding that the full 'women and children first' claim is established.

To assess child prioritization, a separately authorized age-based inquiry with a defined child category would be needed. To assess whether an evacuation practice or order existed or caused outcomes, obtain independent historical documentation of decisions and implementation.
